blog_summary: The blog post discusses a Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) system that learns to play Settlers of Catan, a strategic board game, without being explicitly programmed for it. The author highlights the agent's ability to learn trading strategies, including when to make offers, accept, reject, or counter offers, purely through trial and error guided by a reward function. The key insight is that the DRL agent outperforms heuristic-based and supervised learning opponents, achieving over 50% win rates against heuristic opponents and over 40% against supervised opponents. The author notes that the agent's success demonstrates the potential of DRL for training complex strategic interactive agents, even when trained against random or weaker opponents. The post also draws a parallel between reinforcement learning agents and organizational behavior changes driven by metrics or incentives.
paper_title: Strategic Dialogue Management via Deep Reinforcement Learning
paper_abstract: Artificially intelligent agents equipped with strategic skills that can negotiate during their interactions with other natural or artificial agents are still underdeveloped. This paper describes a successful application of Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) for training intelligent agents with strategic conversational skills, in a situated dialogue setting. Previous studies have modelled the behaviour of strategic agents using supervised learning and traditional reinforcement learning techniques, the latter using tabular representations or learning with linear function approximation. In this study, we apply DRL with a high-dimensional state space to the strategic board game of Settlers of Catan—where players can offer resources in exchange for others and they can also reply to offers made by other players. Our experimental results report that the DRL-based learnt policies significantly outperformed several baselines including random, rule-based, and supervised-based behaviours. The DRL-based policy has a 53% win rate versus 3 automated players (‘bots’), whereas a supervised player trained on a dialogue corpus in this setting achieved only 27%, versus the same 3 bots. This result supports the claim that DRL is a promising framework for training dialogue systems, and strategic agents with negotiation abilities.

figures.title: Settlers of Catan board
figures.caption: The board of the Settlers of Catan game. The board consists of 19 hexes randomly connected: 3 hills, 3 mountains, 4 forests, 4 pastures, 4 fields and 1 desert. Hills produce clay, mountains produce ore, pastures produce sheep, fields produce wheat, forests produce wood, and the desert produces nothing.
